evidence_quotes.quote: This paper reviews current knowledge of the implications of inadequate provision for children’s health and general development
It argues that health education and health care, while essential complements to proper provision, can in no way be considered alternative solutions.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 8 (V. What Level of Provision Do Children Need?)
evidence_quotes.quote: Public latrines are not considered to provide proper access, but shared latrines are. These standards raise the bar in terms of overall quality of provision globally. But the needs of young children and those who care for them are not adequately reflected here.
Distance to water points, regularity of supply and time spent waiting are serious concerns – especially for caregivers dealing with young children.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 14 (VII. The Cost-Effectiveness of Provision)
evidence_quotes.quote: Finally, it is not clear that cost-effectiveness is an appropriate criterion in this case.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community water and sanitation provision in poor urban settlements, including piped household connections, standpipes, water quantity, distance to water points, water storage, and public, shared, and private latrines or sewer connections.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, the paper examines no legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance rule-type mechanism governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure rules, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure). Under the plain wording, it also does not analyse a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor shaping service access; it only critiques international WHO/UNICEF monitoring definitions of 'improved' provision on child-appropriateness grounds and makes normative references to children's rights and cost-effectiveness debates while comparing physical provision against curative health care and hygiene education. Even if those policy/monitoring discussions were read generously under the plain wording, plain_criterion2_decision remains exclude because the paper is non-empirical (E05).
criterion_notes.c3: Narrative literature review and policy essay summarizing selected secondary studies and reports with no primary empirical data collection and no systematic review methodology (no search strategy, inclusion criteria, or structured synthesis). Excluded under E05.
criterion_notes.c4: Treats water and sanitation provision primarily as an environmental determinant of child mortality, diarrhoeal and parasitic morbidity, malnutrition, and cognitive/social development, citing only illustrative secondary statistics on coverage and child latrine usability rather than reporting empirical service-access outcomes of a governance factor.
criterion_notes.c5: Because this is an unstructured narrative overview and policy argument rather than an empirical study or systematic synthesis, there is no identifiable empirical study design, primary sample, or governance-exposure-to-access-outcome analytical design.

study_design: Narrative literature review and policy essay (non-empirical)
country: Global / urban areas in Africa, Asia and Latin America (narrative review; no primary study site)
population_and_sample: Urban children and their caregivers in low-income settlements (narrative overview of secondary literature; no primary sample)
exposure: Inadequate physical water and sanitation provision (contrasted with WHO/UNICEF 'improved' provision definitions, curative medical treatment, and hygiene education)
outcome: Child mortality, diarrhoeal and parasitic morbidity, malnutrition and stunting, cognitive and social development, and practical caregiving burdens
rationale: Excluded as E05 (No empirical evidence). Bartlett (2003) is a narrative literature overview and policy essay examining how inadequate urban water and sanitation provision affects children's mortality, morbidity, nutrition, cognitive/social development, and caregiving burdens, and arguing that WHO/UNICEF 'improved' provision benchmarks, curative health care, and hygiene education are insufficient substitutes for child-appropriate provision. It contains no primary empirical data or methods and is not a systematic empirical synthesis. It also fails Criterion 2 under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, as it does not examine any legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance mechanism governing service access.
